what_its_for: Ocrelizumab is used to treat multiple sclerosis (MS). It works for both relapsing forms of MS (where symptoms come and go) and primary progressive MS (where symptoms slowly get worse over time). It works by targeting and reducing certain immune cells (called B cells) that damage the nerves in your brain and spinal cord.
how_to_take: Ocrelizumab is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly dripped into your vein through a needle. You will receive this treatment at a hospital, clinic, or infusion center. Each infusion takes several hours, so plan to spend most of the day there. Before your infusion, you will be given medicines (such as a steroid, antihistamine, and sometimes a fever reducer) to help prevent reactions. You will be watched closely during and after the infusion for any side effects.
dosing: The usual dose is 600 mg given every 6 months. However, your very first dose is split into two smaller doses of 300 mg each, given 2 weeks apart. After that, you receive a single 600 mg infusion every 6 months. Your doctor will decide the exact schedule that is right for you.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare provider at a clinic, it is important to keep all your scheduled appointments. If you need to reschedule or miss your appointment, call your doctor or infusion center as soon as possible to set up a new time. Do not try to skip doses, as staying on schedule is important for the medicine to work properly.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home. It is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals at your infusion center. However, if you are ever given any supplies to take home, keep them refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C) and protect them from light. Do not freeze. Keep all medicines out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid live vaccines (such as the chickenpox vaccine, MMR, or nasal flu spray) during treatment and until your doctor says it is safe. Talk to your doctor about getting all recommended vaccines before starting treatment. Avoid close contact with people who are sick, as this medicine can weaken your immune system and make it harder to fight infections. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as this medicine may not be safe during pregnancy. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: a fever, chills, or signs of infection (such as a cough, painful urination, or skin sores); signs of an infusion reaction during or after your treatment (such as itching, rash, trouble breathing, dizziness, or fast heartbeat); signs of a serious brain infection called PML (such as confusion, memory problems, vision changes, weakness on one side of the body, or trouble speaking); unusual weakness or numbness; or if you feel your MS symptoms are getting worse. Also tell your doctor if you are pregnant or breastfeeding.
when_it_works: Ocrelizumab does not cure MS, but it can slow down the disease and reduce the number of relapses. Some people notice benefits within a few months, but it may take 6 months or longer to see the full effect. It is important to keep taking this medicine even if you feel well, because it is working to protect your nerves over the long term.
special_populations: Elderly patients: Use with caution, as older adults may have a higher risk of certain side effects. Pregnancy: This medicine may harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose. Talk to your doctor before becoming pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: This medicine is not currently approved for use in children. Hepatitis B: Your doctor will test you for hepatitis B before starting treatment. This medicine can reactivate hepatitis B, which can be life-threatening.
